title: MB7-26183
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: These are my reasons for dismissing the Minister's appeal. I confirm the Refugee Protection Division's (RPD) determination that the Respondent is not excluded from refugee protection and that he is a Convention refugee.

The Respondent, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Haiti. He fears being persecuted due to his sexual orientation because he is gay. Prior to seeking protection in Canada, he lived for several years in the United States (US) before he was deported to Haiti because of his criminal record. History of this case

The Minister intervened in the RPD hearing. The Minister argues that the Respondent is excluded from refugee protection because there are serious reasons for considering he committed a serious non-political crime in the US.
The RPD found the Respondent is not excluded. The RPD went on to determine that the Respondent faces a serious possibility of persecution in Haiti due to his sexual orientation.

The Minister appealed the RPD's decision. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) rejected the Minister's appeal. The Minister asked the Federal Court to review the RAD's decision. The Court found the Minister had been denied procedural fairness and returned the appeal to the RAD for redetermination. This is therefore the rehearing of the appeal of the RPD's original decision. No new evidence or oral hearing
Neither the Minister nor the Respondent have asked to admit any new evidence. I therefore have no jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 The Respondent is not excluded
A person may be excluded from refugee protection where there are serious reasons for considering they have committed a serious non-political crime prior to coming to Canada.2
The Minister's position is that the RPD erred in determining that the Respondent is not excluded. It has not contested the RPD's inclusion analysis.

The Respondent and the Minister were given the opportunity to make submissions after the Court returned this matter to the RAD. I also provided the parties with jurisprudence which I proposed to consider in my exclusion assessment. I put the parties on notice that if I determine the Respondent is not excluded, I may consider inclusion. Submissions were due on 18 February 2025. On 24 February 2025, the Respondent requested an extension of time to respond to the Notice. The Minister has not responded. I find it unnecessary to delay proceedings for further submissions from the Respondent as I have been able to reach a determination based on the material already on record. The application for an extension of time is therefore denied.

I find the Respondent is not excluded because, in my assessment, the crimes he committed in the United States are not "serious". There are serious reasons for considering the Respondent committed offences in the US prior to coming to Canada

The Minister provided evidence to show that the Respondent was convicted of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX offences in the US. There is no evidence that these crimes were connected in any way to a political objective. I find they are not political in nature.

The RPD found the Respondent's testimony credible and preferred it over the documentary evidence submitted by the Minister. It found that, "... the Minister has not credibly established the facts supporting his application for exclusion ...",5 with regard to either incident.

I agree with the Minister that the evidence of convictions meets the threshold of "serious reasons for considering" the Respondent committed offences in the US prior to coming to Canada. What is at issue is whether these offences would be considered "serious" if they were committed in Canada.

paragraphs.text: The Minister does not need to prove that the Respondent was convicted of robbery, merely that there are serious reasons for considering that he committed robbery. This is a relatively low threshold: less than a likelihood but more than a mere suspicion. I find the incident reports which include the statements of the security guards and the fact that the Respondent was originally charged with robbery, even though XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is sufficient to meet this threshold. I find there are serious reasons for considering the Respondent committed offences which would be considered robbery if committed in Canada.
The issue is therefore whether these offences would be considered "serious" in Canada. The offences committed by the Respondent are not serious

An offence punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years is a strong indication that the crime is "serious". Robbery, which is punishable by a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, is generally considered to be serious. However, this ten-year rule should be considered in context of the particular facts of the case and should not be applied in a mechanistic or unjust manner. It is possible to rebut the presumption that robbery is a serious crime.6

Where the criminal provision in Canada has a large sentencing range, the upper end being ten years or more and the lower end being quite low, a person whose crime would fall at the less serious end of the range in Canada should not be presumptively excluded.7 Assessing the seriousness of a crime requires an evaluation of the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction."8 XXXX XXXX 2005 incident Elements of the offence

The elements of robbery in Canada consist of stealing, and for the purpose of preventing or overcoming resistance to the stealing, the use of violence or threats of violence to a person. The use or threat of violence as an element of robbery militates toward its being considered serious. Facts of the offence

Briefly, the facts of this offence are as follows. The Respondent XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX In my assessment, but for the fact that the Respondent XXXX XXXX XXXX, the offence would have been considered a relatively minor theft. In fact, the incident report itself describes it as "shoplifting." Although XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. I find the facts are therefore neutral with respect to the seriousness of the crime. Mode of prosecution

Although the charges in the US were reduced, the Respondent was nonetheless convicted of a felony.9 In Canada, robbery is an indictable offence. Indictable offences are generally more serious than offences which may proceed summarily. I find this a factor which militates towards being considered serious. Penalty prescribed

The Respondent was convicted of the lesser offence of theft against person and sentenced to 7 months. There are reasons why a low sentence may be imposed for a serious crime, such as a plea bargain or a conviction on a lesser offence in return for information. The Minister asserts this robbery charge was reduced to theft as a result of a plea bargain. I see no evidence of any "bargain". The court documents referred to by the Minister show that the prosecutor moved to reduce the charges from a class 2 felony. The Respondent testified that he agreed to plead guilty on his lawyer's advice because it would avoid a robbery conviction and because he had already been in custody for several months. I find on the face of the record that the prosecutor most likely moved for the charges to be reduced because he was of the opinion it was in the interests of justice to do so. There is no evidence that the sentence passed was inordinately lenient or otherwise unjustified as the Minister suggests. I find this is a relatively low sentence which militates toward a finding that the offence is not serious. Mitigating and aggravating circumstances
Neither party has raised any mitigating or aggravating circumstances. Sentencing range

There is a very wide sentencing range for the offence of robbery in Canada. Although there is a maximum penalty of life imprisonment, there is no minimum sentence, except where a weapon is used in the commission of the robbery.10 Use of a weapon is not an issue in this case.

Where there is a wide sentencing range, I need to consider where in that range the crime would fall.11 A person, "... whose crime would fall at the less serious end of the range in Canada should not be presumptively excluded. Article 1F(b) is designed to exclude only those whose crimes are serious."12

The sentencing range is not determinative and is one of many factors. However, I must "look at similar cases as a guide to how the Applicant would be treated in Canada from the sentencing perspective" in order to avoid relying on a subjective notion of what is a serious crime in Canada.13

The maximum sentence, or any significant custodial sentence, is generally reserved for those who, for example, use a weapon to commit the offence, seriously injure another, or participate in a larger criminal scheme. None of these circumstances apply in the Respondent's case. I find that had this offence been committed in Canada, the actual sentence that would be imposed is likely to be far lower than the maximum of imprisonment for life. I find it unlikely that he would face a lengthy period of custody.

The sentencing range imposed in Canada for cases similar to the Respondent's span from receiving a non-custodial sentence up to perhaps several months in custody with lengthier sentences generally in cases where more serious violence or threat of violence is involved.14 In my view, accepting that the Respondent XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his actions would receive a sentence well below the maximum prescribed if committed in Canada. I find it likely he would have received a sentence similar to that actually imposed in the US, in the range of several months' imprisonment. This weighs heavily against a finding that the Respondent's crimes are serious.
When I weigh all of the relevant factors, I find the presumption of seriousness has been rebutted with respect to the first offence in Houston, Texas. XXXX XXXX 2006 incident Elements of the offence

The XXXX XXXX incident does not XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX which would indicate a lengthy custodial sentence or imprisonment for life is warranted. I find that had this offence been committed in Canada, the actual sentence that would be imposed is likely to be far lower than the maximum of imprisonment for life. I find it unlikely that he would face a prolonged period of custody. As noted previously, the Canadian sentencing range for cases similar to the Respondent's span from receiving a non-custodial sentence up to perhaps several months in custody with lengthier sentences generally in cases where more serious violence or threat of violence is involved.15 Again, accepting that the Respondent struck the security guard, his actions would receive a sentence well below the maximum prescribed if committed in Canada, even as a repeat offender. I find it likely he would have received a sentence similar to that actually imposed in the US, in the range of several months' imprisonment. This weighs heavily against a finding that the Respondent's crimes are serious.
When I consider all of the relevant factors, I find the presumption of seriousness has been rebutted with respect to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
For these reasons, the Respondent is not excluded under Article 1F(b) of the Convention and section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Inclusion

The Minister makes no submissions on the RPD's findings with respect to inclusion and that the Respondent is a Convention refugee based on his sexual orientation. I have conducted my own assessment, and I agree with the RPD's assessment. I note that a significant amount of time has passed since the RPD rendered its decision. I have therefore considered the objective documentation with respect to Haiti to determine whether there has been a significant change in circumstances that would warrant coming to a different conclusion.16 I find the situation for sexual minorities in Haiti has not changed significantly since the RPD's determination.

I dismiss the Minister's appeal. The RPD was correct in determining that the Respondent is not excluded from protection and that he is a Convention refugee.
